newsitem.title: UK: Britain jubilant as Labour sweeps to power.
newsitem.headline: Britain jubilant as Labour sweeps to power.

text.p: Britons greeted the prospect of a new Labour government with jubilation on Friday and said it was high time the Conservatives suffered after 18 years of ruling from on high.
"I understand what the Conservatives mean by the feel-good factor -- and I'm finally beginning to feel it," said Andre Spychala, a painter and decorator.
"(Prime Minister) John Major was like a school teacher who couldn't control his class and now term has finished."
"Blinding! Fantastic! Utter joy to see them fall," said James Lucey, a 22-year-old printer.
"The size of the landslide shows the strength of feeling in this country. John Major I consider a liar, his government a bunch of thieves. Finally they have got their come-uppance."
As results trickled in overnight, the extent of Major's drubbing grew ever clearer with voters switching in droves to Tony Blair's centrist Labour Party, out of power since 1979.
The defeat was on a scale unseen for 165 years with Labour -- dragged by Blair from the unelectable left to the prudent centre ground -- on course for a majority of almost 180 seats.
Such a strong backing should allow Britain's youngest leader of the century to grab the reins and rule with confidence for the next five years. The country could barely wait.

"People are desperate for change. Tony Blair has changed his party -- I'm sure he can change Britain as well," said insurance broker Raj Singh. "Britain is facing some big questions with the millenium coming up and Europe a growing issue. We need a strong leader -- and that John Major wasn't."

Indeed, as the sun glowed over Westminster, weary workers who had watched history being made overnight spoke time and again of the need for a new start from a government lazy from power, out of touch with voters and arrogant in its self-belief.
"Ah but it's nice to see them go down. They have been crushing the people for so long they felt power was theirs forever," said taxi driver Stanley Syta.

"Power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. What a relief to see that lot gone," said Kathleen Mally, a 63-year-old housemaid at the upper House of Lords. "Oh my God, that was 18 years too long -- there will be jubilation in the Lords today and utter relief they are gone. It can't get worse."
All around parliament, drunken revellers circled in pursuit of parties and sober civil servants scurried into ministries knowing a new boss was on the way with the change of government.
"I'm a happy man this morning. More than anything I wanted change and I hope that's what I get with everyone saying they're one and the same now," said Dav Hayre, a Treasury employee.

Hayre said he hoped the arrival of a new boss in the finance ministry, expected to be Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown, would mean less privatisation and more job security than under the current Chancellor Kenneth Clarke.
"But there's been no change for so long that nobody even knows if there will be a goodbye to Clarke do or a meet Gordon Brown session. I just hope my job will be safer now," he said.
A 56-year-old Foreign Office worker said he too was pleased to see the back of the establishment party.
"They deserved all they got. The Conservatives are the most arrogant people I have ever come across -- and I have been a Conservative voter since I was 21," he said.
"They are motivated by pure self-promotion, never the country, and you can see the country is now behind Blair."
But a 40-year-old colleague -- a lone sceptic on Whitehall among the throng of new Labourites questioned -- said Britain should prepare for a return to the evil ways of old Labour.

"We will see the re-introduction of the word "comrade' and you will see the hard left exhale in anticipation," he said. "One can only hope I'm wrong and that Tony Blair is a man of his word. If not, a con-trick of massive proportions has been perpetrated on the British people."
